text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.
LES ECHOS
-- UGC cinemas chairman opposes idea of a uniform price for cinema tickets, says plans is to invest one billion francs in cinemas in France and in Spain.
-- Luxury goods group LVMH sells one-third of stake in Guinness for 5 billion francs, retains a 14 percent stake.
-- Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade expects operating profits seen in 1996 to continue in 1997.
LA TRIBUNE

-- Workers at Credit Foncier occupy building and hold governor since Friday to protest Finance Minister Jean Arthuis's decision to transfer part of its activity to Credit Immobilier de France and wind group down.
-- Bosses of small and medium firms less pessimistic in January, survey shows.
-- Culture minister Philippe Douste-Blazy calls for a cut in value-added tax VAT on recorded music.
-- Credit Lyonnais does not rule out cutting a further 2000 jobs through the year 2000 as part of its restructuring plan.
-- PSA carmaker chairman confirms he expects a 9.5 percent drop in the French automobile market for 1997.
L'AGEFI
-- Export insurance body Coface expects economic growth in the next century to concentrate around the Pacific Ocean, while Western Europe is seen as the main export target in world trade.
-- Large firms call for a balance between pension funds and staff savings schemes.
LE FIGARO-ECONOMIE
-- Trade minister Jean-Pierre Raffarin to consider allocating part of planned pension funds to small and medium-sized firms.
-- Zodiac expected to bounce at Paris bourse in 1997.
LIBERATION (Economic section)
-- Senate to look tomorrow at planned reform of SNCF railway operator that includes a transfer of railroad ownership and maintenance to a new structure.
THE INTERNATIONAL HERALD TRIBUNE

-- Bundesbank governor says in an interview that economic hardships in Germany and Europe stem from failing to implement economic reforms needed to match the rising power of Asia, the growth of Eastern Europe and the dynamic revival of the United States. He adds European governments should not link needed spending cuts, labour market deregulation and welfare reform to Maastricht criteria and the building of a European single currency, as it is making the issue unpopular.
